newsitem.title: GERMANY: Duisenberg endorses timely EMU on German visit.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg endorses timely EMU on German visit.

text.p: Wim Duisenberg, Dutch central bank president and incoming head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), on Friday put his weight behind a timely launch of Europe's planned single currency.

Duisenberg, in Germany for a meeting with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, said Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would go ahead on schedule on January 1 1999 without any weakening of the entry criteria for the project.
At the same time, Duisenberg noted that longer term economic developments in would-be EMU states would also be important when judging which countries could participate in the first leg.

The Maastricht Treaty "takes into account the mid-term economic development of a would-be member state, looking ahead to 1998 and further," he told a news conference at the headquarters of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) party.

The issue of sustainable fulfilment of EMU convergence criteria has gained in significance in recent months as more and more signs emerge that key European Union countries will struggle to meet Maastricht criteria on the nail.

Economists are viewing with increasing scepticism Germany's insistence that it can cut its budget deficit this year to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), below the crucial Maastricht threshold of three percent.

EMU contenders will be picked early next year on the basis of 1997 data and partially on the basis of recommendations submitted by the EMI, where Duisenberg is to replace Alexandre Lamfalussy as president later this year.

Duisenberg's visit also earned him an endorsement as the best candidate to be first president of the European Central Bank, which comes into being next year to oversee the launch of the euro in 1999 and to steer monetary policy in the euro region thereafter.
"As far as I know, there is only one candidate for the presidency of the European Central Bank and I know of no better candidate than Wim Duisenberg," Waigel said.
Waigel also said it would benefit Europe should Britian decide to take part in monetary union.

"Britain will decide for itself whether to take part in EMU, but it would be good for Europe and Britain if it takes part," Waigel told a news conference at the party headquarters of his Christian Social Union (CSU).

Asked about the implications for the euro of the British Labour party landslide victory in Thursday's elections, Waigel said he did not wish to interfere in the country's domestic politics but said the anti-EMU line taken by the Conservative party had not paid off.
Waigel said in recent years he had had good cooperation with the new British Chancellor of the Exchequer, Labour's Gordon Brown, and said he struck him as interested in fiscal stability.
